title: Boosting I - AdaBoost
abstract:
The first boosting algorithm. AdaBoost combines many weak learners —
models barely better than chance — into a strong one, by training them
sequentially and forcing each to focus on the mistakes of the last. This document
covers weak learners and decision stumps, the $\{-1,+1\}$ labelling and why it is
used, the derivation of the model weight $\alpha$ and the sample-weight update,
the aggregation rule, the hyperparameters, and AdaBoost's defining weakness:
sensitivity to noisy labels.

blocks.t: Weak Learners and Stumps
From the notes

items:
Weak learners — an ML model with accuracy just over
 50%. In AdaBoost we combine multiple weak learners together.
 A D.T with max_depth $=1$.

Decision stumps — a type of weak learner. In AdaBoost
 we use decision-stump weak learners.

Classification is on $(-1,1)$, not $(0,1)$ like other
 classification.

We boost the misclassified points before sending them to the next
 stage, by upsampling.
Uses sequential learning.
Each model tries to correct the errors of the previous one.

Assigns weights to all data points, with higher weightage to the
 misclassified points.
This forces the next model to focus more on the mistakes.

blocks.cap:
Three stages of AdaBoost. Point size is the sample weight; circled
 points were misclassified and are upsampled for the next stage. The final panel
 shows the weighted combination, which is far more expressive than any single
 stump.

blocks.t:
With labels in $\{-1,+1\}$ the product $y_i h(x_i)$ is $+1$ when correct and $-1$
when wrong, so a single expression $e^{-\alpha y_i h(x_i)}$ handles both
cases — it shrinks the weight when correct and grows it when wrong. With
$\{0,1\}$ you would need a case split at every step. It also makes the final
prediction simply the sign of the weighted sum.
The Algorithm
The three steps of each stage
Initialise $w_i=1/n$. For $m=1,\ldots,M$:

items:
Fit a stump $h_m$ on the data using the current weights $w$, and
 compute its weighted error
 $$\varepsilon_m=\frac{\sum_i w_i\,\mathbb{1}\!\left[h_m(x_i)\neq y_i\right]}{\sum_i w_i}.$$

Compute its say — the notes' "$\alpha$ calculated based on
 performance":
 $$\boxed{\;\alpha_m=\frac{1}{2}\ln\!\left(\frac{1-\varepsilon_m}{\varepsilon_m}\right)\;}$$

Update the weights — upsample the mistakes:
 $$\boxed{\;w_i \leftarrow w_i\,e^{-\alpha_m y_i h_m(x_i)}\;} \quad\text{then normalise.}$$

blocks.t: Final prediction:
\boxed{ H(x)=\operatorname{sign} \left(\sum_{m=1}^{M}\alpha_m h_m(x)\right) }

blocks.cap:
Left: $\alpha$ as a function of the weighted error. Right: the weight
 multiplier — correct points are scaled by $e^{-\alpha}$ and mistakes by
 $e^{+\alpha}$.

blocks.t: Reading $\alpha$

head: $\varepsilon_m$
$\alpha_m$
Meaning
rows: Random guessing — no say at all
Worse than random — negative say, so its vote is flipped

blocks.t:
This is exactly the notes' "$\alpha$ calculated based on performance".
Note the elegance of the $\varepsilon=0.5$ case: a coin-flip learner receives zero
weight automatically, so it cannot damage the ensemble.
Where $\alpha$ comes from
AdaBoost is stagewise minimisation of the exponential loss

L=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp \left(-y_i F(x_i)\right),
 \qquad F(x)=\sum_m \alpha_m h_m(x).
Adding a stump $h$ with weight $\alpha$ gives

L(\alpha)=e^{-\alpha} \sum_{\text{correct}} w_i + e^{\alpha} \sum_{\text{wrong}} w_i
 = e^{-\alpha}(1-\varepsilon)+e^{\alpha}\varepsilon .
Setting $dL/d\alpha=0$:

-e^{-\alpha}(1-\varepsilon)+e^{\alpha}\varepsilon=0
 \Longrightarrow 
 e^{2\alpha}=\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}
 \Longrightarrow 
 \alpha=\tfrac12\ln\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}.

And the new weight of point $i$ is its contribution to that loss,
$w_i e^{-\alpha y_i h(x_i)}$ — so the weight update is not a heuristic either.
Both formulas fall out of one optimisation.
Hyperparameters
From the notes

Controls how much importance each model

Left: test accuracy against the number of stumps. Middle: the learning
 rate. Right: AdaBoost's defining weakness — as labels are corrupted it

blocks.t: The two interact

The learning rate $\nu$ scales every $\alpha_m$, so a smaller $\nu$ means each
stump contributes less and more stumps are needed. They trade off almost
exactly: halving the learning rate roughly doubles the required
n_estimators. Tune them together, and prefer a small $\nu$ with many
estimators — it generalises better, at more compute.
The Weakness
Exponential loss makes AdaBoost chase noisy labels

The weight of a point grows as $e^{\alpha}$ every time it is misclassified. A
mislabelled point can never be classified correctly, so its weight grows
exponentially, round after round, until the ensemble is devoting most of its
capacity to fitting an error.

This is the direct consequence of using exponential loss, which penalises large
margins violations far more harshly than log loss does. It is why:

items:
AdaBoost degrades sharply with label noise, while bagging degrades
 gracefully;
outlier removal (Topics 28–30) matters more here than for most models;

Gradient Boosting (Topic 67) — which generalises boosting to
 any differentiable loss, including robust ones — superseded it.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Reduces bias — turns weak learners into a strong one
Sensitive to noisy labels and outliers
Slower to train than bagging for the same count
Resistant to overfitting in practice, even at large $M$

blocks.t: Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import AdaBoostClassifier, RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score, GridSearchCV

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 10))
y_01 = (1.5*X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] - .8*X[:, 2] + .6*X[:, 0]*X[:, 1]
        + rng.normal(0, 1.1, n) > 0).astype(int)
y = np.where(y_01 == 1, 1, -1)                  # labels in {-1, +1}
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3,
                                          stratify=y, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. A WEAK LEARNER: A DECISION STUMP
# =====================================================================
stump = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"single stump accuracy: {stump.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}   "
      f"(a weak learner -- 'just over 50%')")
print(f"deep tree accuracy   : "
      f"{DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"200 boosted stumps   : "
      f"{AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 2. ADABOOST FROM SCRATCH -- the three steps of each stage
# =====================================================================
def adaboost(X, y, M=200):
    n = len(X)
    w = np.ones(n) / n                          # equal weights to start
    models, alphas, history = [], [], []

    for m in range(M):
        # STEP 1: fit a stump using the CURRENT weights
        h = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=0)
        h.fit(X, y, sample_weight=w)
        pred = h.predict(X)

        eps = np.sum(w[pred != y]) / np.sum(w)   # weighted error
        eps = np.clip(eps, 1e-10, 1 - 1e-10)

        # STEP 2: alpha, "calculated based on performance"
        alpha = 0.5 * np.log((1 - eps) / eps)

        # STEP 3: UPSAMPLE the mistakes  w <- w * exp(-alpha * y * h(x))
        w = w * np.exp(-alpha * y * pred)
        w /= w.sum()

        models.append(h); alphas.append(alpha)
        history.append((eps, alpha, w.max() / w.min()))
    return models, np.array(alphas), history

def ada_predict(models, alphas, X):
    agg = sum(a * h.predict(X) for a, h in zip(alphas, models))
    return np.sign(agg)                          # sign of the weighted sum

models, alphas, hist = adaboost(X_tr, y_tr, M=200)
print(f"\nscratch AdaBoost: {(ada_predict(models, alphas, X_te) == y_te).mean():.4f}")
print(f"sklearn AdaBoost: "
      f"{AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=200, algorithm='SAMME', random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")

print(f"\n{'stage':>6s} {'weighted err':>13s} {'alpha':>8s} {'max/min weight':>16s}")
for m in [0, 1, 2, 5, 20, 100, 199]:
    e, a, r = hist[m]
    print(f"{m+1:6d} {e:13.4f} {a:8.4f} {r:16.1f}")
# The error rises towards 0.5 as the problem gets harder, alpha falls, and
# the weight ratio grows -- later stumps see a very skewed distribution.

# =====================================================================
# 3. ALPHA IS THE MODEL'S "SAY"
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'error':>8s} {'alpha':>10s}  meaning")
for e in [0.01, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.99]:
    a = 0.5*np.log((1-e)/e)
    note = ("huge say" if a > 1 else "no say at all" if abs(a) < 1e-9
            else "NEGATIVE -- vote flipped" if a < 0 else "moderate say")
    print(f"{e:8.2f} {a:10.4f}  {note}")
# err = 0.5 gives alpha = 0: a coin-flip learner is automatically ignored.

# =====================================================================
# 4. THE WEIGHT UPDATE UPSAMPLES THE MISTAKES
# =====================================================================
w = np.ones(8) / 8
yt = np.array([1, 1, 1, 1, -1, -1, -1, -1])
pr = np.array([1, 1, 1, -1, -1, -1, 1, -1])      # 2 mistakes
alpha = 0.5*np.log((1-0.25)/0.25)
w_new = w * np.exp(-alpha * yt * pr); w_new /= w_new.sum()
print(f"\nalpha = {alpha:.4f}")
print(f"{'point':>6s} {'correct?':>9s} {'w before':>10s} {'w after':>9s} {'ratio':>7s}")
for i in range(8):
    print(f"{i:6d} {str(yt[i]==pr[i]):>9s} {w[i]:10.4f} {w_new[i]:9.4f} "
          f"{w_new[i]/w[i]:7.2f}")
# Mistakes are scaled UP by e^alpha; correct points DOWN by e^-alpha.
print(f"the 2 mistakes now carry {w_new[yt!=pr].sum():.1%} of the total weight")

# =====================================================================
# 5. IT REDUCES BIAS -- the whole point of boosting
# =====================================================================
def bias_variance(make, sims=100):
    grid = rng.normal(0, 1, (300, 10))
    truth = (1.5*grid[:,0] + grid[:,1] - .8*grid[:,2] + .6*grid[:,0]*grid[:,1] > 0)
    P = []
    for _ in range(sims):
        Xi = rng.normal(0, 1, (500, 10))
        yi = (1.5*Xi[:,0] + Xi[:,1] - .8*Xi[:,2] + .6*Xi[:,0]*Xi[:,1]
              + rng.normal(0, 1.1, 500) > 0).astype(int)
        P.append(make().fit(Xi, yi).predict(grid))
    P = np.array(P)
    return np.mean((P.mean(0)-truth)**2), np.mean(P.var(0))

print(f"\n{'model':26s} {'Bias^2':>9s} {'Variance':>10s}")
for tag, mk in [("single stump (HBLV)", lambda: DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1)),
                ("AdaBoost, 200 stumps", lambda: AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=200,
                                                                    random_state=0))]:
    b2, v = bias_variance(mk)
    print(f"{tag:26s} {b2:9.4f} {v:10.4f}")
# Bias COLLAPSES; variance rises a little. Boosting attacks BIAS --
# the mirror image of bagging (Topic 60).

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE HYPERPARAMETERS, AND HOW THEY INTERACT
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'n_est':>6s} {'lr':>6s} {'cv acc':>9s}")
for ne, lr in [(50, 1.0), (200, 1.0), (200, 0.5), (400, 0.25), (800, 0.1)]:
    s = cross_val_score(AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=ne, learning_rate=lr,
                                           random_state=0),
                        X_tr, y_tr, cv=4, n_jobs=-1).mean()
    print(f"{ne:6d} {lr:6.2f} {s:9.4f}")
# Halving the learning rate roughly doubles the estimators needed --
# they trade off almost exactly.

gs = GridSearchCV(AdaBoostClassifier(random_state=0),
                  {"n_estimators": [100, 300, 600],
                   "learning_rate": [0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0],
                   "estimator": [DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1),
                                 DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2)]},
                  cv=4, n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\nbest: {gs.best_params_}  cv {gs.best_score_:.4f}  "
      f"test {gs.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 7. THE WEAKNESS -- noisy labels
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'% labels flipped':>17s} {'AdaBoost':>10s} {'RandomForest':>14s}")
for f in [0.0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30]:
    yn = y_tr.copy()
    flip = rng.random(len(yn)) < f
    yn[flip] = -yn[flip]
    a = AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, yn).score(X_te, y_te)
    r = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0,
                               n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, yn).score(X_te, y_te)
    print(f"{f:17.0%} {a:10.4f} {r:14.4f}")
# AdaBoost falls away much faster: a mislabelled point can never be
# classified correctly, so its weight grows as e^alpha every single round.

yn = y_tr.copy(); flip = rng.random(len(yn)) < .10; yn[flip] = -yn[flip]
_, _, h_noisy = adaboost(X_tr, yn, M=100)
print(f"\nwith 10% noise, max/min weight ratio after 100 stages: {h_noisy[-1][2]:.0f}")
print(f"without noise:                                          {hist[99][2]:.0f}")
# The ensemble ends up devoting most of its capacity to fitting errors.

# =====================================================================
# 8. SEQUENTIAL, SO NOT PARALLELISABLE
# =====================================================================
import time
for tag, m in [("AdaBoost (sequential)", AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=300,
                                                            random_state=0)),
               ("RandomForest, n_jobs=1", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300,
                                                                 random_state=0, n_jobs=1)),
               ("RandomForest, n_jobs=-1", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300,
                                                                  random_state=0, n_jobs=-1))]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); m.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{tag:26s} {time.perf_counter()-t0:.2f}s")
# AdaBoost has no n_jobs for the boosting loop -- stage m+1 needs stage m's
# weights. Bagging parallelises perfectly; boosting cannot.
Worked Examples
One AdaBoost round, with the weight update
Points $x = [1,2,3,4,5]$, labels $y = [+1,+1,-1,-1,+1]$. Start with uniform weights $w_i = 0.2$. The weak learner is a stump: predict $+1$ if $x \le 2.5$, else $-1$.
Step 1 – weighted error. The stump misclassifies only $x=5$ (label $+1$, predicted $-1$):
\varepsilon = \sum_{i:\text{wrong}} w_i = 0.2
Step 2 – the stump's vote.
\alpha = \tfrac12 \ln\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon} = \tfrac12 \ln 4 = 0.693
A stump with low error gets a large say in the final vote.
Step 3 – reweight. Correct points: $w \leftarrow w\,e^{-\alpha}$; wrong points: $w \leftarrow w\,e^{+\alpha}$. Since $e^{\alpha} = 2$:
Step 4 – normalise (sum is $0.8$, divide by it):
The misclassified point now carries half the total weight. The next stump is forced to get $x=5$ right, which is the whole idea of boosting: focus on what the previous learners got wrong.
Final prediction is $\operatorname{sign}\big(\sum_t \alpha_t h_t(x)\big)$, a weighted vote of all stumps.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
A weak learner has accuracy just over 50%; AdaBoost
 combines multiple weak learners. It uses decision
 stumps — a decision tree with max_depth $=1$.

Classification is on $(-1,1)$, not $(0,1)$, so that
 $y_i h(x_i)$ is $\pm1$ and one formula covers both cases.

It uses sequential learning: each model tries to correct
 the errors of the previous one.

It assigns weights to all data points, with higher weightage to
 the misclassified points, which forces the next model to focus
 more on the mistakes. We boost the misclassified points before
 sending them to the next stage, by upsampling.

$\alpha_m=\frac12\ln\frac{1-\varepsilon_m}{\varepsilon_m}$ is
 calculated based on performance: $\varepsilon=0.5$ gives
 $\alpha=0$ (no say), low error gives a large say, and worse-than-random
 gives a negative say.

Weight update $w_i\leftarrow w_ie^{-\alpha_m y_ih_m(x_i)}$; final
 prediction $\operatorname{sign}\left(\sum_m\alpha_mh_m(x)\right)$.

Both formulas are the stagewise minimiser of the exponential
 loss — neither is a heuristic.

Hyperparameters: n_estimators (number of weak iterations),
 learning_rate (how much importance each model gets),
 random_state.

Boosting attacks bias. Its weakness is sensitivity to
 noisy labels, because a mislabelled point's weight grows exponentially.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. How does AdaBoost work?

Start with equal weights. Fit a stump, compute its weighted error, and give it a
say $\alpha=\frac12\ln\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$. Multiply the weights of
misclassified points by $e^{\alpha}$ and correct ones by $e^{-\alpha}$, so the
next stump concentrates on the mistakes. Repeat, and predict by the sign of the
$\alpha$-weighted sum.
Q. Why decision stumps?

Because boosting reduces bias, so it wants high-bias, low-variance base
learners it can compose. A deep tree already has low bias and high variance, which
is bagging's raw material, not boosting's. Stumps are also fast, and their
weakness is exactly what the sequential correction repairs.
Q. Why are the labels $\{-1,+1\}$?

So that $y_ih(x_i)$ equals $+1$ when correct and $-1$ when wrong, letting the
single expression $e^{-\alpha y_ih(x_i)}$ both shrink and grow weights. It also
makes the final prediction the sign of the weighted sum.
Q. Where does the $\alpha$ formula come from?

It is not a heuristic. AdaBoost performs stagewise minimisation of the exponential
loss $\sum_i e^{-y_iF(x_i)}$; differentiating with respect to $\alpha$ and setting
to zero gives $e^{2\alpha}=(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon$. The weight update is the
same optimisation, expressed per point.
Q. What happens if a weak learner has 50% error?

$\alpha=0$, so it contributes nothing — the ensemble automatically ignores a
coin flip. Below 50%, $\alpha$ is negative and its vote is inverted, which is
also correct.
Q. Why is AdaBoost sensitive to noisy labels?

Because a mislabelled point can never be classified correctly, so its weight is
multiplied by $e^{\alpha}$ every round and grows exponentially. Eventually the
ensemble devotes most of its capacity to fitting that error. Bagging averages
noise away instead; gradient boosting with a robust loss (Topic 67) is the modern
answer.
Q. Can AdaBoost be parallelised?

No. Stage $m+1$ needs the weights produced by stage $m$, so the boosting loop is
inherently sequential. Bagging and random forests parallelise perfectly — one of
the practical reasons to prefer them when training time matters.
